setup: Use a bench high enough for the plates to hang free
Lie face down, chest at the top edge
Overhand grip, a bit wider than your shoulders
Let the bar hang on straight arms
execution: Pull the bar up to the underside of the bench
Keep your chest down on the pad
Lower under control to straight arms
faults: Don't lift your chest off the bench
Don't shrug your shoulders to your ears
Don't drop or bounce the bar off the floor
Don't kick your legs to help the pull

notes: Check the bench is stable and rated for your bodyweight plus the bar before you lie on it; a home-made bench on boxes or plates must not rock.
Set the bar where you can reach it from the bench, and lower it to the floor or stands under control at the end of the set.
Climb on and off the bench carefully; the bar is under your face, so never let go of it mid-rep.
If pain lingers or comes back, stop this exercise and get it checked by a physio or doctor.
stopIf: Pain that changes how you move

regressions.name: Chest-supported machine row
regressions.reason: Guided path and stack loading; no bar to handle from a high bench.

regressions.name: Chest-supported dumbbell row
regressions.reason: Same supported row on an incline bench with a pair of dumbbells; no tall bench needed.

progressions.name: Paused seal row
progressions.reason: A pause with the bar against the bench removes any swing.

substitutions.name: Dumbbell seal row
substitutions.reason: Same bench and position with a pair of dumbbells; load is each dumbbell and the range can be a bit longer.

substitutions.name: Chest-supported dumbbell row
substitutions.reason: Chest supported on an incline bench; load is each dumbbell.

substitutions.name: Chest-supported machine row
substitutions.reason: Supported row on a machine; easy to load in small steps.

substitutions.name: Barbell row
substitutions.reason: Same bar and pull without support; more lower-back and hamstring demand.

substitutions.name: Seated cable row
substitutions.reason: Horizontal pull on a stack when no tall bench is free.

guideBrief.cameraNote: Side view at bench height. Bench along the floor line, figure lying face down with the head at the near end; the bar seen end-on under the chest. Plates must clear the floor at the bottom.

keyPositions.label: Bottom
keyPositions.describe: Lying prone on a tall flat bench, chest at the top edge, legs along the bench. Arms hang straight down holding the bar under the shoulders; plates just clear of the floor.

keyPositions.label: Halfway
keyPositions.describe: Elbows bending and travelling up beside the body, bar rising in a near-vertical line. Chest stays on the pad.

keyPositions.label: Top
keyPositions.describe: Bar touching or close to the underside of the bench. Elbows above the torso line, shoulder blades pulled together and down. Chest and hips still on the pad.

ikHints: Torso fixed horizontal on the bench pad
Hands fixed to the bar about 1.2× shoulder width
Bar travels vertically under the shoulders
guideBrief.barPath: Close to vertical, from straight arms up to the underside of the bench
emphasise: Chest stays on the bench throughout
Elbows lead the pull up past the torso
Bar stops at the underside of the bench

sources.title: Catalyst Athletics Exercise Library: Bench Row (seal row, chest-supported row)

uncertain.note: A seal row needs a flat bench tall enough for the plates to hang clear of the floor (a dedicated seal-row bench, or a flat bench raised on stable blocks). There is no station value for that yet, so `bench` is used; the gym's ordinary flat bench is usually too low for a loaded barbell.

"Seal row" alone is used for both the barbell and the dumbbell version (Catalyst lists both), so it is not an alias here: a FitNotes "Seal Row" is suggested as this entry for Ben to confirm, never matched. No dumbbell seal row entry yet.

"Chest-supported barbell row" and "Prone barbell row" are deliberately not aliases: both names are also used for a face-down row on an incline bench, with a different torso angle and range. An import shows them as a Check (never matched) and Ben chooses (review import-names-r2 S1).
Approximate drawing targets, not measured data. Shoulder flexion is measured from the arm hanging along the torso line; the torso is horizontal here.
